etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English erect, a borrowing from Latin ērectus (“upright”), past participle of ērigō (“raise, set up”), from ē- (“out”) + regō (“to direct, keep straight, guide”).

definitions.definition: Upright; vertical or reaching broadly upwards.

quote.citation: 1788, Edward Gibbon, chapter LXIV, in The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, volume VI, London:  […]  W[illiam] Strahan; and T[homas] Cadell, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Among the Greek colonies and churches of Asia, Philadelphia is still erect—a column in a scene of ruins.

definitions.definition: (of body parts) Rigid, firm; standing out perpendicularly, especially as the result of stimulation.
(of a person) Having an erect penis or clitoris.
(obsolete) Bold; confident; free from depression; undismayed.

quote.citation: 1827, [John Keble], The Christian Year: Thoughts in Verse for the Sundays and Holydays throughout the Year, volume (please specify |volume=I or II), Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  [B]y W. Baxter, for J. Parker; and C[harles] and J[ohn] Rivington, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: But who is he, by years / Bowed, but erect in heart?

quote.citation: 1715, [Alexander] Pope, The Temple of Fame: A Vision, London:  […]  Bernard Lintott […], →OCLC, page 23:
quote.text: His piercing Eyes, erect, appear to vievv / Superior VVorlds, and look all Nature thro'.

quote.citation: 1594–1597, Richard Hooker, edited by J[ohn] S[penser], Of the Lawes of Ecclesiastical Politie, […], London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby [for Matthew Lownes], published 1611, →OCLC, (please specify the page):

definitions.definition: (heraldry) Elevated, as the tips of wings, heads of serpents, etc.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English erecten, from the adjective (see above).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To put up by the fitting together of materials or parts.
(transitive) To cause to stand up or out.
(intransitive, aviation, of a gyroscopic attitude indicator) To spin up and align to vertical.
To raise and place in an upright or perpendicular position; to set upright; to raise.
(transitive) To lift up; to elevate; to exalt; to magnify.

quote.citation: 1595, Samuel Daniel, “(please specify the folio number)”, in The First Fowre Bookes of the Ciuile Wars between the Two Houses of Lancaster and Yorke, London:  […]  P[eter] Short for Simon Waterson, →OCLC:

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:

quote.text: I, who am a party, am not to erect myself into a judge.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To animate; to encourage; to cheer.

quote.citation: a. 1678 (date written), Isaac Barrow, “(please specify the chapter name or sermon number). Of Contentment”, in The Works of Dr. Isaac Barrow. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to VII), London: A[braham] J[ohn] Valpy, […], published 1830–1831, →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (transitive, astrology) To cast or draw up (a figure of the heavens, horoscope etc.).

quote.citation: 1971, Keith Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic, Folio Society, published 2012, page 332:
quote.text: In 1581 Parliament made it a statutory felony to erect figures, cast nativities, or calculate by prophecy how long the Queen would live or who would succeed her.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To enter a state of physiological erection.

quote.text: On the 17th of July, the patient returned to the country, perfectly healed: the penis erected and he was capable of coition.
